items.title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
items.titleZh: 世界不会等待：在实时时钟下评估和教导代理商
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0--100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

items.title: Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation
items.titleZh: 在基准饱和后评估模型能力
items.summary: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.

items.title: Value-Informed Schedule Trimming for Accelerated Sequential Monte Carlo Guidance in Discrete Diffusion
items.titleZh: 离散扩散中用于加速顺序蒙特卡罗引导的价值知情进度调整
items.summary: Reward-guided discrete diffusion enables test-time alignment with downstream objectives, but applying Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance at every denoising step is computationally expensive. Active guidance steps require additional reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations. Sparse guidance reduces this cost by guiding only a subset of timesteps, but commonly used schedules are fixed heuristics whose effectiveness can vary substantially across tasks. We propose VISTA, a training-free method that automatically selects guided timesteps under a fixed budget. VISTA formulates sparse guidance as approximation of the ideal full-guidance probability path and derives an estimable upper bound on \(\ell_1\) path deviation. Using value statistics collected from a small number of full-guidance warmup generations, VISTA optimizes the resulting empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming. The warmup generations can be retained as model outputs, and after schedule selection VISTA has the same per-generation guidance complexity as other sparse schedules with the same budget. Across text, biological sequence, and image generation tasks, VISTA discovers task-dependent schedules and outperforms hand-designed sparse schedules in most tested settings, while approaching or exceeding full-guidance performance on several task metrics. In toxic-text generation, for example, VISTA attains a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio compared with 1.00 for full guidance while reducing post-selection per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35$\times$ speedup.

items.title: AlphaDiana: A Measurement System for Agents in Verifiable Reasoning Tasks
items.titleZh: AlphaDiana：可验证推理任务代理的测量系统
items.summary: Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and retain history in memory. Understanding agent performance requires linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. We introduce AlphaDiana, a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers. It preserves harness-native control loops while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately. AlphaDiana supports macro analyses of complete agents and micro interventions on agent components such as tools, skills, and memory under matched conditions. We study three open-source models and three open-source harnesses on five answer-based benchmarks, with two models also tested on two interactive benchmarks. We find that harnesses do not consistently improve the accuracy of reasoning: gains on questions unsolved by the model alone can be outweighed by losses on questions it answers correctly without tools. This inconsistency extends to component interventions: neither skill guidance nor retained history reliably improves accuracy. Behavior and output-token use must be assessed with correctness: low token entropy can accompany wrong answers, and less output per execution can mean more output tokens per correct answer when accuracy falls. AlphaDiana links answer correctness and execution status to traces and resource records for comparing agents and diagnosing failures under shared task and resource policies.

items.title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
items.titleZh: 由于国际化输入错误， Anthropic控制台向我的卡多收了100倍的费用
items.summary: I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline. The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04. Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD. To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge. Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism: Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback": 1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge. 2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk. 3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now. The Support Wall: I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform. As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable. If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem. Pura vida! R.S.G.

items.summary: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check-automated or human-is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look.
